summary: Lists requirements for gathering and transferring location information securely while protecting the privacy of the people involved. It focuses on authorization, security and privacy needs, in particular for the Geopriv Location Object and the protocols that use it. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Apps that know where you are can be useful, but they can also expose you. This document lists what a system must do so that location data is only shared under rules the user sets, and only in a protected form.

subtitle: What a secure, privacy-respecting way to share a person's location must provide.

tldr.problem: Location services need to gather and pass on where someone is, but sharing location can expose that person's privacy.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets requirements for a Geopriv Location Object and the protocols that carry it: user-set Privacy Rules, support for unlinked pseudonyms, and fields for authentication, integrity, confidentiality and replay protection.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document, not a protocol, and it has been updated by RFC 6280 and RFC 7459.

facts.label: Location data types
facts.value: At least 1; RFC says SHOULD be 2 (coordinates, civil)

today: RFC 3693 is an Informational requirements document, not a protocol, and it has been updated by RFC 6280 and RFC 7459. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Overview and Guiding Principles
sections.content:
Location-based services, such as navigation, emergency services and tracking equipment in the field, need the geographic location of a Target (a user, a resource or another entity). Collecting and transferring that information has privacy implications, so the document focuses on the authorization, security and privacy requirements for these services.

Six principles guide the requirements. The Location Object must be securely transmitted, with the sender and receiver authenticated and the object itself protected. User-controlled Privacy Rules, set by the Rule Maker (usually the user), decide who may receive location and for what purpose. Rules can filter location by reducing precision or resolution (a co-worker might learn only the city). The Location Object should be able to carry a limited core set of rules. Where appropriate, location should not be tied to a real identity. And the user may want to hide identities even from other protocol participants.
sections.plainLanguage: You should decide who learns where you are, and how precisely. A co-worker might learn only your city, never your street.

sections.title: The Four Primary Geopriv Entities
sections.content:
The basic architecture has four entities. The Location Generator (LG) initially determines or gathers the Target's location and creates Location Objects. The Location Server (LS) receives published Location Objects, applies the Privacy Rules it learns from the Rule Holder, and notifies recipients. The Location Recipient (LR) receives notifications of Location Objects. The Rule Holder (RH) houses the Privacy Rules for specific Targets; a Location Server may pull rules from it, or rules may be pushed to it.

The rules in the Rule Holder are populated by the Rule Maker, and the RFC says rules MUST be authenticated and protected. The entities need not be separate machines: the interfaces could be internal to one device, and in some designs the Location Generator, Rule Holder and Location Server are all implemented in the same device.
sections.plainLanguage: One component finds you, a gatekeeper decides what to reveal, someone receives the result, and a rulebook holds your settings. A single device can play several of these roles at once.

sections.title: Sightings, Location Objects, Rules and Pseudonyms
sections.content:
The first determination of location from non-public information is a Sighting: an abstract pair of (Identifier, Location). A sighting may be transformed before anyone outside sees it, so the identifier becomes a pseudonym and the location loses precision or resolution.

The Location Object (LO) conveys the Target's location information together with an identity or pseudonym of the Target, time information, core Privacy Rules, authenticators and more. Most fields are optional, including the location itself. A using protocol is one that reads or modifies the LO; a protocol that only carries it as a string of bits is a transport protocol.

A Privacy Rule regulates collection, use, disclosure and retention of location information, and the RFC says rules must be obeyed, not treated as advisory. An unlinked pseudonym is a name whose link to its holder is, at least initially, unknown to anyone except the holder or a trusted server. Flows are trusted when a pre-existing contract covers location privacy, and non-trusted otherwise. The RFC also lists four situations that might override the Rule Maker: emergency services, legal interception, an employer or location owner, and a government in non-emergency cases. Only the emergency case has to be facilitated.
sections.plainLanguage: The location note is an envelope that can carry a stand-in nickname instead of your real name, plus a rulebook that must be followed. The rules say who may see the note, how precise it is, and how long it may be kept.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
For the Location Object: Geopriv MUST define one LO that every entity supports, it MUST be extensible, usable in protocols such as HTTP and SIP as well as local APIs, and usable securely on constrained devices. The LO definition MUST contain fields for the Target identifier, the recipient's identity, credential and proof of possession, the location, the location data type, timing information, a rule field, security headers and trailers, and a version number. At least one location data type MUST be supported by all receivers, and the RFC says there SHOULD be two: latitude, longitude and altitude coordinates, and civil locations such as city, street and number.

For rules-based transfer: a Location Server's decision to give a recipient location MUST be based on the Rule Maker's Privacy Rules. A Location Generator MUST follow the Rule Maker's instructions even without access to the full rules, for example by sending the LO only to a URI the Rule Maker designates. Geopriv MUST specify a limited rule language, and MAY specify a full one.

For security: the LO MUST support unlinked pseudonyms in the identification fields, and fields for mutual end-point authentication, data integrity, confidentiality and replay protection. Geopriv MUST specify a minimum mandatory-to-implement set of cryptographic algorithms, and the protocol SHOULD allow a bypass if authentication fails during an emergency call. One stated non-requirement: bridging to non-IP networks such as the PSTN.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule list says the location note must be extensible, sealed against tampering and replay, and able to hide your real name. The gatekeeper may only reveal location under the rules you set, even when the finder only knows part of those rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Only the information inside the Location Object is protected under the Rule Maker's rules; headers and other objects generally are not, so Geopriv may not defend the Target against general traffic analysis. Privacy Rules are secured according to where they live: rules in a non-public Rule Holder are typically authenticated with a message authentication code or a signature, rules in a public Rule Holder are typically digitally signed, and rule fields inside an LO are secured with the LO itself.

For emergency calls where authentication fails, the Rule Maker could write a rule to send the location anyway or to let the call fail; when the user cannot authenticate, a reasonable default is to send the location only to an emergency center. Unlinked pseudonyms are needed for anonymity, and hiding the identity of the Location Recipient from the Location Server prevents inferences about the Target's habits from who asks. The RFC also notes Unintended Targets, such as the driver of a tracked rental car, whose privacy is affected even though the company only tracks the vehicle.
sections.plainLanguage: The seal covers the location note itself. Someone watching who sends messages to whom could still learn things, so the design adds tricks such as nicknames that change and hidden recipients.

sections.title: Issues Left for Later
sections.content:
The RFC lists questions deferred to later documents. A Location Object may hold one or several location fields, each with one or more representations of the same position, such as different formats or sightings at different times. Fields could show that one location is a translation of another, with the translator identified.

The LO MUST NOT carry a truth flag: Geopriv must be silent on whether the location information is true. The format of timing information is out of scope. Who defines identifiers is still open: letting the using protocol define the name space makes embedded authentication easier, while letting the Rules choose gives the user control of anonymity. The RFC notes that pseudonyms should be changed regularly, because identifying the person behind an unlinked pseudonym can be very simple.
sections.plainLanguage: Some questions went into a to-do pile, such as how to write down the time. One answer is firm: the note may never claim to be telling the truth about your location.
